Ten killed in Russian attack on drone exhibition near Kyiv
- Published
At least 15 people have been killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine, including 10 dead in ballistic missile strikes on an exhibition near Kyiv showcasing drone technology.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said some 100 people had been injured in the daytime attack on the exhibition, attended by prominent members of the defence sector.
Five people were also killed by Russian glide bombs in the eastern city of Sloviansk. Early on Saturday, military officials confirmed the deaths of two men in the northern city of Sumy.
On Friday evening, Zelensky said he had received intelligence that Russia was preparing another massive missile strike, which could happen "within the next 48 hours".
A Ukrainian strike on Friday killed six people and wounded 26 in the Russian city of Kirov, more than 1,000km (600 miles) behind the front line. Ukraine also attacked warehouses of Wildberries - Russia's biggest online retailer.
After the attacks near Kyiv, there were initially fears for the safety of Defence Ministry adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov, also known as Flash, and Lyuba Shypovych, who has been involved in developing technology for the Ukrainian army.
Following the incident, both took to social media to confirm they were unharmed, and Beskrestnov said he had stayed away from the event because of security concerns.
Ukrainian air force spokesman Yuri Ihnat told Ukrainian TV the attack involved three ballistic missiles, only one of which was intercepted.
Russia confirmed the attack. Its Defence Ministry said high-precision long-range weaponry had been used on a site where drones for use in targeting civil sites in Russia were being demonstrated.
It said producers of drones, as well as representatives of Ukraine's drone forces and security services "directly planning and carrying out strikes on Russian territory" were present.
This is at least the third time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 that an exhibition of this kind has been hit.
There has been widespread outrage that a public event of this kind was being held at all and had, apparently, been widely advertised.
President Zelensky said the incident was being investigated, while Ukraine's prosecutor-general said efforts were under way to establish who decided to hold the event and what safety measures were in place.
The attack came hours after the Ukrainian strikes on a factory in the city of Kirov and warehouses in north-west Russia.

Wildberries is the Amazon of Russia. Ukraine is trying to destroy it
Ukraine has used drones to destroy vast warehouses full of goods
For a week now, Ukrainian drones have been attacking vast warehouses that are a crucial part of Russia's biggest online retailer, Wildberries.
Logistics hubs in St. Petersburg were hit overnight Thursday. Video verified by CBC News and Reuters show multiple drones exploding as they crash into the facilities, leading to fires that appear to have totally destroyed the warehouses. It's estimated that billions of dollars worth of goods have gone up in flames.
The attacks started last weekend, one in the town of Kotovsk, some 360 kilometres from the border with Ukraine, and another in the city of Elektrostal, about 50 kilometres east of Moscow. Nine people were killed and 80 others wounded.
More attacks happened early Wednesday. Ukrainian drones struck Wildberries warehouses in Krasnodar and Stavropol. Verified video of those incidents spread widely on social media.
The strikes on Wildberries warehouses were confirmed by company founder Tatyana Kim in statements after the attacks, as well as Russian officials.
At least seven warehouses have been struck so far.
What is Wildberries?
Wildberries is often referred to as the equivalent of Amazon in Russia. By some estimates, it accounts for half of all online sales in the country.
Wildberries was launched in 2004 by Kim, a teacher and a young mother at the time, focused, at first, on selling clothes.
Since then, the platform has become an industry leader and household name, allowing big and small businesses alike to sell their goods to customers across the country by storing, shipping and delivering their inventory. In April, Forbes Russia estimated Kim's fortune at $8.1 billion US.
Kim has said that last year, the company had more than 200 logistics facilities totaling over 5.2 million square metres, with plans to build new warehouses this year in Belarus and Kazakhstan, where Wildberries operates as well. It also operates in Russian-held Crimea.
Does Wildberries supply military equipment?
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy did not name Wildberries directly, but he said the facilities his country attacked were involved in supplying gear and various technical components to the Russian military.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Tuesday that "it is not the case" and accused Kyiv of continuing to "strike civilian targets."

corpus.title: Wildberries Freezes Loan Repayments for Merchants After Drone Strikes
corpus.signal_text:
E-commerce giant Wildberries announced Friday that it has frozen loan repayments for small and medium-sized businesses whose inventory was destroyed in recent Ukrainian drone attacks on its warehouses.
The three-month payment pause will apply automatically through the company’s in-house financial services through the end of October. The relief builds on existing financial support provided through the retailer’s parent company Wildberries & Russ (RWB).
Wildberries previously announced a broader merchant relief package, including reduced storage fees, promotional discounts for select products and waived regional transit charges.
On Thursday, RWB said that around 88,000 individual merchants began receiving the first tranche of compensation payments for products destroyed during a Ukrainian attack on its fulfillment center in the Moscow region.
However, some merchants have complained online that the payouts fell well short of the value of their lost goods, according to an analysis of seller chat groups by the exiled news outlet Agentstvo.
The Moscow region fulfillment center was among the first Wildberries facilities hit last Saturday. A wave of subsequent strikes has targeted multiple other warehouses, knocking out an estimated 10% of the company’s logistics capacity, Kommersant reported.
Ukraine has accused Wildberries of supplying the Russian military with drone parts and other equipment. The company has denied the claim.
Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim, Russia’s wealthiest woman, promised financial aid to the families of employees killed or injured in the attacks.
Just days before the strikes began, Wildberries updated its merchant agreement to exempt itself from financial liability for products damaged or destroyed in missile and drone attacks. Other Russian e-commerce platforms have since done the same.
